paper_title: LociArt: A Unified Paradigm for Free-Style Local Video Stylization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video stylization typically transforms entire scenes, while local artistic editing requires precise region--style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency. We introduce LociArt, a unified paradigm for free-style local video stylization that explicitly specifies where to stylize and what style to apply while preserving non-target content. At its core, GRNStyle builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) and introduces a polar style-aware mask that embeds style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions. Complementary representation--geometry conditioning combines encoded mask features with raw-mask spatial support, integrating spatiotemporal context with geometric control. To provide paired supervision, we develop an automated pipeline combining global stylization, video object removal, matting, and compositing, and construct the LociArt-100K Dataset with 100K local stylization pairs. We further establish the LociArt Benchmark, comprising 80 source videos and 84 target masks covering 168 foreground/background stylization cases, with a Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) evaluation scheme for regional style quality and complementary measures of non-target preservation and temporal consistency. Experiments show that GRNStyle outperforms existing methods in regional style quality and spatial control while maintaining strong temporal consistency. Qualitative examples further illustrate joint stylization of multiple regions with the same or different learned styles, despite training only on single-region, single-style pairs. Together, these components provide a unified foundation for learning and evaluating controllable local video stylization. Project page: https://higherhu.github.io/lociart/.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Video stylization transforms recorded footage into artistic renditions for film, advertising, and digital art. Building on image style transfer [1, 2] and diffusion-based image generation and editing [3, 4], video methods use text or reference images to guide appearance while preserving motion [57]. Yet artistic control often requires more than global transformation: an artist may turn moving subject into sketch within an otherwise unchanged scene, reimagine the surroundings as watercolor while keeping the subject intact, or bring distinct artistic styles to different objects in the same shot, as shown in Fig. 1. We call this task free-style local video stylization: controlling both where to stylize and what style to apply across space and time, while preserving non-target content. Video segmentation provides practical starting point. few user interactions can define masks that propagate across frames, with streaming inference supporting real-time processing [8, 9]. Such masks offer an accessible spatial prior for local stylization [10, 11], extending control from foreground subjects to the less-explored task of stylizing their surroundings. Yet selecting region does not specify its artistic transformation: binary mask indicates editing extent but not style identity. With style supplied separately through text, the model must learn to associate the intended appearance with the selected region. Reliable local control also requires preserving region boundaries throughout motion. Despite advances in attention supervision [12, 13] and mask-conditioned editing [1417], mask representations face trade-off between spatiotemporal context and spatial fidelity. VAE-based processing aligns masks with learned video features [18], but compression can blur their geometry; direct resampling retains spatial structure without the same learned temporal context [19]. Thus, useful conditioning mechanism must both bind styles explicitly to regions and retain the spatial detail needed to localize their effects over time. These modeling challenges are compounded by gaps in supervision and evaluation. Training pairs must demonstrate local artistic changes, faithful preservation elsewhere, and natural transitions along moving boundaries. Global stylization pairs [7, 20] do not directly supply this supervision, while instruction-based video-editing datasets [13, 21] cover broader editing operations. Likewise, global similarity and video-averaged scores can conceal weak regional style, changes outside the target, and transient failures. Free-style local video stylization therefore calls for coordinated advances in paired data, regionstyle conditioning, and region-aware evaluation. We introduce LociArt, unified paradigm addressing these needs through the LociArt-100K Dataset, the GRNStyle model, and the LociArt Benchmark. Our automated data pipeline combines global stylization, video object removal, matting, and compositing to construct 100K curated pairs. Each example contains source video, an editing mask, style instruction, and locally stylized target, supervising transformation and preservation together. Constructing these targets requires handling contour changes introduced by stylization. Object removal supplies clean background content for newly exposed areas, while alpha mattes estimated separately for original and stylized objects guide compositing along their respective contours, avoiding object remnants and enabling natural boundary transitions. Trained on these pairs, GRNStyle builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) [22] and the source-evidence editing formulation of GRNEdit [23]. Its core design is polar style-aware mask, which embeds style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions, unifying where to stylize and what style to apply without imposing scalar ordering on styles. Complementary representationgeometry conditioning combines VAE-encoded mask features with raw-mask spatial support to integrate spatiotemporal context and geometric control, while source evidence guides content preservation throughout refinement. To evaluate local stylization, the LociArt Benchmark contains 80 source videos and 84 object mask units, each evaluated under both foreground and background stylization protocols, yielding 168 stylization cases. It uses Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) to measure regional style fidelity, together with complementary measures of non-target preservation and temporal consistency. Our contributions are threefold: Unified Paradigm for Local Video Stylization. We introduce LociArt, unified computational paradigm that formulates local video stylization as region-conditioned artistic transformation, explicitly specifying where to stylize and what style to apply while preserving non-target content and temporal consistency. GRNStyle with Style-Aware Region Control. We propose GRNStyle, GRN-based model that unifies region and style through polar style-aware masks and combines spatiotemporal context with geometric control. Qualitative examples further illustrate free-style multi-region, multi-style compositions learned from single-region, single-style supervision. Scalable Data Construction and Region-Aware Evaluation. We develop an automated pipeline to construct the LociArt-100K Dataset and establish the LociArt Benchmark with 80 source videos and 84 objectmask units, integrating SPS with preservation and temporal consistency measures for region-aware evaluation.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Image style transfer. Neural style transfer progressed from per-image optimization [1] to feed-forward arbitrary transfer with AdaIN [2]. Building on latent diffusion [3], StyleShot [24] separates style from content, while TeleStyle [25] learns content-preserving transfer from curated triplets and extends it to video. Localized editing, however, requires explicit spatial control. Localized stylization. Image methods use masked feature or attention control [16], masklearned regional attention [12], or semantic-region matching [11]. For video, Xia et al.[26] use spatiotemporal alignment, while UniVST [10] combines mask propagation, AdaIN-guided latent and attention manipulation, and optical-flow smoothing without training. In contrast, we study locally artistic video stylization with paired supervision and fixed, equal-norm polar codes that bind style identity to editable regions. Video stylization and generative editing. PickStyle [27] learns lightweight style adapters from synthetic clips derived from paired images. VISTA [7] and MoStyle [28] use style/source/stylizedvideo triplets; DreamStyle [20] supports text-, image-, and first-frame-guided stylization from paired videos. For broader editing, VACE [14] unifies video conditions including masks, while VideoPainter [15] performs context-conditioned inpainting. Beyond diffusion, GRN [22] uses binary-state refinement, and GRNEdit [23] treats the source as editing evidence. GRNStyle extends this evidence-based formulation by combining VAE-encoded mask features with raw-mask 3 Figure 2 Overview of the data construction pipeline. Source and object-removed videos are globally stylized and filtered, then combined through mask-guided matting to produce foregroundand background-stylized pairs for human verification. geometry, thereby coupling temporal semantics with spatial fidelity. Data and evaluation. Ditto-1M [21] scales instruction-based editing, while CoinVE-200K and CoinVE-Bench [13] target compositional editing, including regional stylization. StyleShot [24] and MegaStyle [29] provide image data for stylistic consistency and diversity; StyleShot also introduces StyleBench. Evaluation spans image quality with ArtFID [30], style similarity with CSD [31], and video quality and temporal consistency with VBench [32]; RegionRoute [12] also evaluates regional style and background preservation. LociArt-100K adds pairs aligning content, regions, styles, and targets; its benchmark measures regional style, non-target preservation, temporal consistency, and VLM-based perceptual quality.

sections.title: 3 LociArt-100K Dataset Construction
sections.content: To supervise local stylization and non-target preservation, we construct the LociArt-100K Dataset of 100K pairs by separating global style generation from spatial composition. Specifically, we globally stylize source and object-removed videos, then recombine their components into complementary foreground and background targets. Each example contains source video Vsrc, binary editing mask M, style instruction 𝑝, and locally stylized target Vsty. As illustrated in Fig. 2, the pipeline comprises the following four steps. Step 1: Object identification and removal. We first identify the objects to separate from their surroundings. Source videos are collected from SA-V [8] and Ditto-1M [21]. Qwen3-VL-32B [33] identifies salient objects, and their category prompts guide SAM3 [9] to produce temporally tracked masks Mobj. After vision-language, temporal-coverage, and area checks, each accepted mask guides SVOR [19] to remove the selected object, yielding Vrem. This reconstructed background fills areas exposed by stylization-induced contour changes, avoiding original-object remnants during compositing. Appendix Section A.1 details the mask selection and filtering procedures. 4 Step 2: Global stylization and filtering. With source and reconstructed background videos available, we run both Ditto [21] and our internal fine-tuned VACE [14] on each under stylization instruction 𝑝. For either global stylizer 𝐺, we get two stylized outputs: sty src = 𝐺(Vsrc, 𝑝), sty rem = 𝐺(Vrem, 𝑝). (1) Before using these outputs for local composition, GPT-5.5 is used to assess style quality, content preservation, and temporal quality through two cascaded gates: the source-video pair is evaluated first, followed by the object-removed pair. Only candidates passing both proceed to matting and compositing. More details appear in Appendix Section A.2. Step 3: Matting and localized compositing. We next localize the accepted stylizations. Since stylization can change object contours, we use VideoMaMa [34] to estimate separate alpha mattes sty Asrc and Asty from Vsrc and src with the same tracked mask Mobj, respectively. These mattes follow the respective object boundaries through time and are used for compositing instead of binary masks. The resulting composites stylize the foreground while retaining the background, or vice versa: sty fg = Asty sty bg = Asrc Vsrc + (1 Asrc) Here denotes element-wise multiplication, with alpha values broadcast across color channels. Both targets are paired with Vsrc and 𝑝. The directional editing mask is = Mobj for the foreground target and = 1 Mobj for the background target. sty src + (1 Asty) Vrem, sty rem. (2) Step 4: Human verification. Finally, because compositing may introduce artifacts, annotators inspect each completed example for content preservation, boundary quality, and temporal consistency. Only qualified samples are retained, yielding final dataset of 100K video pairs covering 18 style categories. More details on the verification and final dataset statistics can be found in Section A.3.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Training. We train the 2B GRNStyle model on LociArt-100K with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs, using all 18 styles unless otherwise specified. We fully fine-tune the backbone and conditioning branches. More training details are provided in Appendix Section D. Benchmark. We introduce the LociArt Benchmark for local video stylization; it contains 80 source videos and 84 object-mask units. Each videomask pair is evaluated under two complementary stylization protocols: foreground stylization edits the tracked foreground-object mask Mobj, while background stylization edits its complement 1 Mobj. The benchmark therefore contains 168 cases in total. More details can be found in Appendix Section C.1. Metrics. We use SPS (Style Prototype Similarity) to measure whether the edited region matches the requested style using prototype bank in the CSD [31] feature space. Regional CLIP-T (CLIPT) [37] measures alignment between the edited region and the canonical style phrase, while PSNR [38] measures fidelity to the source in the non-target region. TC (Temporal Consistency) [39] measures cosine similarity between CLIP embeddings of adjacent frames. Additionally, we use Gemini 3.6 Flash to provide separate Style and Preserve scores for regional stylization quality and non-target content preservation. Detailed definitions and implementation protocols are provided in Sections C.2 to C.4.

sections.title: 5.2 Comparison with Existing Methods
sections.content: We compare with methods spanning regional image stylization and video editing: LEAST [35], UniVST [10], RegionRoute [12], and StyleGallery [11] are image-based methods, whereas VACE1.3B [14], CoinVE-Edit [13], and the commercial system Seedance 2.5 [36] target video generation or editing. LEAST and StyleGallery directly composite the non-edited region from the source using the mask, while others generate or reconstruct the complete output; accordingly, PSNR is not reported for the former two because source-pixel copying makes it non-comparable. To isolate the contribution of task-specific supervision, we additionally fine-tune VACE-1.3B on LociArt-100K using the same architecture-independent hyperparameters as GRNStyle. Quantitative and perceptual comparison. As shown in Table 1, GRNStyle achieves the best SPS for both foreground (0.407) and background (0.705) stylization, together with the best 8 Figure 4 Qualitative comparison of local video stylization. Examples evaluate stylization inside the editing region, preservation outside it, and temporal consistency. Foreground and background cases highlight leakage, distortion of preserved content, and boundary inconsistency. GRNStyle produces localized styles with coherent boundaries and stable non-target content. background CLIPT (0.199). It also maintains strong preservation, with the second-best background PSNR (26.15 dB) and near-best temporal consistency (TC: 0.983). The VLM scores further indicate favorable balance between regional stylization and non-target preservation, achieving the highest Style score (4.62) while retaining high Preserve score (4.64). The highest PSNR values from VACE coincide with its minimal stylization, so they do not indicate better stylepreservation trade-off. In addition, Appendix shows that GRNStyle remains competitive with SOTA global stylization methods under all-one masks. Qualitative comparison. Fig. 4 presents representative resultsof local video stylization. GRNStyle renders the armchair and room in pixel art while preserving the dog, and adds pencil strokes to the bear without desaturating the surrounding rocks, demonstrating precise regional stylization and faithful preservation. Other methods tend to produce weak edits, spill stylization beyond the target, or lose subject detail. Additional examples are provided in Appendix I.

sections.title: 5.3 User Study
sections.content: We conducted user study with 20 participants on 160-case subset (16 cases per style), with each case receiving one rating from this participant pool. Since the study evaluates generated videos, we compare GRNStyle only with the two video-based methods, CoinVE-Edit and Seedance 2.5. As shown in Fig. 5(a), GRNStyle achieves the highest mean ratings for style fidelity (4.34) and background preservation (4.47), indicating stronger artistic expression together with better scene preservation. Fig. 5(b) further shows consistent benefits across styles: GRNStyle outperforms CoinVE-Edit on both criteria for all ten styles, improves preservation over Seedance 2.5 for every style, and improves style fidelity for seven styles.

sections.content: To examine whether predefined polar codebook limits expansion to new styles, we extend separately trained 10-style model to 15 styles using only the five new classes and no replay of the original data. The polar and binary variants follow the same protocol, and retention is measured against their respective 10-class checkpoints. sections.title: 5.6 Effect of the Data Construction Pipeline
sections.content: To assess the contribution of each data-construction step, we compare direct mask compositing, using object removal but no matting, and the complete pipeline for both foreground and background stylization. As shown in Fig. 7, background editing with direct compositing can leave ghost curls or head outlines when stylized subjects extend beyond their source silhouettes; object removal eliminates these artifacts. For foreground editing, source-aligned masks may clip stylized curls, hair tips, and noses, while removal alone cannot resolve the mismatch. Matting follows the actual foreground contour, preserving fine boundaries and providing cleaner supervision for style-induced shape changes.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced LociArt, unified framework comprising automated data construction, the LociArt100K dataset, GRNStyle, and region-aware benchmark. Built on GRN, GRNStyle combines representationgeometry conditioning with polar style codes to balance spatial control and temporal context while preserving non-target content, outperforming the evaluated baselines on the LociArt Benchmark. Category-aware polar style-aware masks further enable zero-shot multi-region compositions from single-region, single-style supervision, reducing the need for exhaustive paired data. Limitations and future works are discussed in Appendix Section H.

sections.title: A Detailed Data Pipeline
sections.content: All videos are standardized to 81 frames at 720p resolution. Frame correspondence is maintained throughout object removal, global stylization, matting, and compositing, so source, removed, stylized, and alpha videos remain aligned. Both Ditto [21] and our internal fine-tuned VACE [14] are run on the source and object-removed videos; each stylizer produces candidate outputs for the subsequent quality checks. A.1 Object Inventory and Mask Filtering Details This stage identifies candidate foreground objects and obtains reliable masks for object removal and subsequent local composition. We first build an object inventory, track the selected instances, and then filter their masks for semantic correctness and temporal coverage. Object inventory. Qwen3-VL-32B [33] analyzes each source video to identify prominent foreground objects, excluding broad background regions such as sky, roads, and walls. Each inventory entry contains concise category label and an appearanceand location-based description. The category label provides the prompt for segmentation. Instance handling. Using these category prompts, SAM3 [9] produces temporally tracked instance masks. When several objects share category, their masks remain separate if their identities can be reliably tracked, preserving object-specific control for the later removal and compositing steps. Mask filtering. We then use Qwen3-VL-32B [33] to reject missing, flickering, or incorrectly assigned masks. Additional checks require nonempty masks in more than 40% of frames and reject masks whose maximum per-frame area exceeds 85% of the frame. Temporal coverage counts all nonempty frames, not the length of continuous track. These production thresholds select masks with sufficient visibility and bounded foreground extent before object removal. A.2 Global Stylization Quality Filtering Details The source and object-removed videos provide complementary content for local composition, so both stylizations must preserve their inputs while expressing the requested style. We assess them through two cascaded gates with shared sampling and scoring protocol, retaining only candidates that satisfy the acceptance criteria below. Cascaded evaluation. The source-video pair is evaluated first; failure at this gate stops processing for the candidate. Passing candidates proceed to evaluation of the object-removed pair, and both pairs must pass before matting and compositing. To avoid repeated evaluation, source-gate results are reused for candidates sharing the same source, style instruction, and actual stylized output. Removal-gate results are cached separately for each object-removed video, style instruction, and corresponding stylized output. Distinct removal inputs or generated outputs require separate evaluations, even when the source video and style are shared. Frame sampling and scoring. At either gate, we sample frame indices 0, 20, 40, 60, and 80 from the aligned 81-frame videos. GPT-5.5 receives ten images in chronological paired order, with an original and stylized frame at each time point. It scores style adherence, content preservation, structural quality, style consistency, and temporal quality on 15 scale. Acceptance criteria. The resulting five scores must reach 4, 4, 3, 4, and 4, respectively. In addition, pair is rejected if it introduces salient objects, removes or duplicates objects, changes semantics or identity, inserts text or logos, or exhibits major layout changes, severe deformation, or ghosting. The total score is reported for reference only and imposes no additional passing threshold. Evaluation prompt. The following prompt (Listing 1) implements the same sampling, scoring, and acceptance protocol for both gates, with the corresponding input video and stylized output supplied in each case. A.3 Human Verification Details After matting and compositing, human review checks the completed local edits for failures that global stylization filtering may miss. Reviewers assess each sourcemaskinstructiontarget example against the criteria below, then retain qualified pairs to form the final dataset. Listing 1 VLM prompt for global stylization quality filtering. You are strict content-preservation evaluator for full-video stylization result. Target production style: {production_prompt} Canonical style category: {style_category} The input videos contain 81 aligned frames (indices 0 through 80). You receive 10 images from five uniformly sampled time points in chronological paired order: - Images 1 and 2: ORIGINAL frame 0 and STYLIZED frame 0 - Images 3 and 4: ORIGINAL frame 20 and STYLIZED frame 20 - Images 5 and 6: ORIGINAL frame 40 and STYLIZED frame 40 - Images 7 and 8: ORIGINAL frame 60 and STYLIZED frame 60 Figure 8 Representative rejection cases from the data pipeline. - Images 9 and 10: ORIGINAL frame 80 and STYLIZED frame 80 Each original/stylized pair is the same time point. Compare every pair and use all five time points. Do not decide from the first pair alone. Evaluate the requested style while preserving semantic content strictly. Content preservation includes the same people, animals, objects, object count, identities, roles, actions, interactions, scene layout, camera view, and major background structures. Do not penalize normal style transformations such as changed colors, simplified details, stylized facial features that preserve identity, painterly/cartoon/anime/clay/pixel/vector rendering, or moderate texture simplification. However, be conservative: if an object identity, person identity, object count, action, or scene layout cannot be confidently matched between an original/stylized pair, score content_preservation below 4 and reject. Do not assume an ambiguous or redesigned object is preserved. Reject new salient person/object, disappearance or duplication, an object changing semantic category, identity/role/gender change, action transfer, major layout change, inserted text/logo/ graphic, severe deformation, or ghosting. Judge style adherence against the explicitly requested target style, not against generic stylization or photorealism. Examples: - Low Poly requires visible facets/polygonal shading. - Pixel Art requires block-like pixels and limited palette. - Claymation requires plasticine material and rounded clay forms. - Oil Painting requires painterly brushwork. - Watercolor requires translucent washes. - Anime or Ghibli requires recognizable hand-drawn animation treatment. - Other styles must show their characteristic visual language. Score exactly these five dimensions from 1 to 5: - style_adherence - content_preservation - structural_quality - style_consistency - temporal_quality Passing criteria: - style_adherence >= 4 - content_preservation >= 4 - structural_quality >= 3 - style_consistency >= 4 - temporal_quality >= 4 - hard_reject_reasons must be empty Report total as the sum of the five scores for reference only; it is not an additional passing criterion. Return ONLY one valid JSON object. Do not output analysis, Markdown, or any text outside the JSON object: { "pass": false, "style_adherence": 1, 18 (a) Style-category distribution (b) Foreground-object mask area ratios Figure 9 Statistics of the LociArt-100K Dataset. The 100K qualified pairs cover 18 style categories. Area ratios refer to foreground object masks Mobj, not the complementary background editing masks. "content_preservation": 1, "structural_quality": 1, "style_consistency": 1, "temporal_quality": 1, "total": 5, "hard_reject_reasons": [], "reason": "Brief evidence-based explanation" } Verification requirements. qualified sample must satisfy four requirements: (i) the requested style is expressed while semantic content, object identities and counts, actions, and scene layout remain consistent with the source; (ii) non-target content is preserved without unintended style spillover; (iii) masks and compositing boundaries remain coherent, without incomplete regions or visible unstylized remnants; and (iv) the video is temporally consistent, without frame breakage or flicker. These checks distinguish unintended content changes from valid artistic transformations: style-consistent changes in color, texture, detail, and object contours are permitted. Acceptance and archiving. Candidates meeting all four requirements are labeled qualified and retained; those failing the checks are rejected and discarded. Typical rejection cases include weak or incorrect style, semantic or identity changes, inserted or missing objects, unintended changes to preserved content, incomplete masks, and temporal artifacts. Representative examples rejected during human verification are shown in Fig. 8 and our demo page: https://higherhu.githu b.io/lociart/. Production statistics. The pass rate is 52.4% for global stylization VLM filtering and 65% for human verification of the resulting local composites. These rates are measured at their respective filtering stages. sections.title: C Details of the Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: We first describe the construction and evaluation units of the LociArt Benchmark, then assess local stylization along three complementary axes: regional style, measured by Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) and regional CLIPT; temporal consistency and non-target preservation, measured by temporal consistency (TC) and regional PSNR; and full-video perceptual quality, measured by the VLM Style and Preserve scores. C.1 Benchmark Construction and Evaluation Units The benchmark contains 80 source videos and 84 object-mask units, each with 81 aligned frames. Videos with two selected subjects contribute separate object-mask units. Of the 80 videos, 13 come from the rejected Ditto [21] pool and were excluded from our training data, 46 come from the DAVIS 2017 training split [40], and 21 come from Pexels1. The foreground area ratios range from 0.02 to 0.58, and 29 units contain human subjects. We denote the tracked foreground-object mask by Mobj and the directional editing mask by M, with = Mobj for foreground editing and = 1 Mobj for background editing. Throughout the metric definitions below, 𝑁 denotes the number of frames in the evaluated aligned sequence and 𝑛 {1, . . . , 𝑁} indexes frame; for benchmark clips, the nominal sequence length is 81. 1https://www.pexels.com/ 21 (a) Style prototype visualization. (b) Row-normalized confusion matrix under leave-one-source-out validation, achieving 93.61% macro-averaged accuracy. In the quantitative and perceptual comparison, all methods Styles and comparison coverage. receive the same input videos for the same target style and follow the same frame-alignment protocol for shared cases. Table 4 lists the 18-style vocabulary and the ten-style comparison subset (bench10). Each object-mask unit supports foreground and background editing, so the complete ten-style grid contains 84 10 2 = 1,680 results (168 cases, 10 styles). C.2 Regional Style Metrics C.2.1 Localized Region Construction Both SPS and regional CLIPT operate on localized region rather than the full output frame. Let be an output video and Mobj its tracked foreground-object mask. VideoMaMa [34] maskguided matting of the output yields foreground alpha video Aout, allowing localization to follow stylization-induced contour changes. For foreground stylization, each frame is cropped to the alpha-support bounding box with 2% margin. For background stylization, the full frame is retained while foreground-object tokens are excluded from the region representation, avoiding an artificial filled foreground area. Thus, SPS and regional CLIPT share the same localization rule and differ only in how the localized region is scored. To test whether SPS distinguishes the 18 style categories beyond source-specific appearance, we perform leave-one-source-out validation: all samples derived from the held-out source video are excluded when constructing its reference prototypes. Each frame is assigned the style of its nearest prototype by cosine similarity, and frame predictions are aggregated by video-level majority vote. This yields macro-averaged classification accuracy of 93.61%. Fig. 10b shows the class-wise confusion matrix, complementing the prototype visualization in Fig. 10a. Together, these analyses characterize the prototype organization and support SPSs ability to distinguish the evaluated style categories. 23 C.2.3 Regional CLIPT Regional CLIPT measures alignment with the canonical style phrase, complementing SPSs visual prototypes. Using the same localized region construction as SPS, it extracts image and text features with CLIP ViT-L/14 [37]. Let 𝜒𝜔 (Y𝑛, Aout,𝑛) denote the region image embedding and let 𝜂𝑠 denote the CLIP text embedding of the canonical phrase for style 𝑠 in Table 4. Then CLIPTreg,𝑛 = cos(cid:0)𝜒𝜔 (Y𝑛, Aout,𝑛), 𝜂𝑠(cid:1) , CLIPTreg = 1 𝑁 𝑁 𝑛=1 CLIPTreg,𝑛. (15) As with SPS, video-level means are averaged before dataset aggregation. The alpha video defines region selection; it is not itself the RGB image passed to the image encoder. SPS and regional CLIPT therefore differ in their scoring encoders and similarity targets, not in their spatial localization rule. C.3 Temporal and Preservation Metrics C.3.1 Temporal Consistency Following AVID [39], TC (Temporal Consistency) uses full-frame image embeddings 𝒛𝑛 from CLIP ViT-H/14 tower, separate and larger encoder than the ViT-L/14 used for regional CLIPT: TC = 1 𝑁 𝑁 1 𝑛=1 cos(𝒛𝑛, 𝒛𝑛+1), 𝒛𝑛 = CLIPimg(Y𝑛). (16) TC summarizes adjacent-frame feature consistency over the aligned output sequence. It is global measure and does not replace regional style or preservation scores. C.3.2 Non-Target Preservation Preservation is measured with regional PSNR [38] outside the intended edit. For foreground stylization, PSNR is computed on the preserved background region 1 M; for background stylization, it is computed on the preserved foreground region M. In both cases, the valid region is derived from the foreground alpha in Aout on an 8-bit scale: the preserved background core comprises pixels with alpha at most 5, whereas the preserved foreground core comprises pixels with alpha above 200. The anti-aliased transition band in between is excluded. We compare aligned output and source frames after resizing the source to the output resolution and use the common valid temporal range. For each frame, the RGB reconstruction error is averaged over the valid non-edit pixels and channels, and the resulting errors are aggregated over valid frames before conversion to PSNR. Frames with insufficient valid pixels are skipped; when an alpha estimate is empty, the original mask is used as fallback. C.4 VLM Evaluation We use Gemini 3.6 Flash to complement the objective metrics with full-video VLM assessment of two separate quantities: Style (edit_region_style) and Preserve (non_edit_preservation). Each is an integer from 0 to 5. The scores are not merged, so strong stylization cannot compensate for damage to non-target content, or vice versa. This evaluation is distinct from the GPT-5.5 data-construction filter, which uses five dimensions on 15 scale. Inputs and execution. The judge receives the source video first and the edited result second, aligned frame by frame and tagged SRC and RESULT. red contour marks the foreground object in the source. For foreground editing, its interior is the target; for background editing, the exterior is the target. The text instruction explicitly identifies the direction, and the contour and display tags are not scored. We use the English system prompt and rubric below with temperature zero. Responses are parsed as JSON; if parsing fails, the same request is retried once. Scoring anchors. Style jointly assesses style correctness, coverage of the edit region, and crossframe stability. score of 5 requires all three, 3 indicates visible but imperfect style, incomplete coverage, or occasional flicker, and 0 indicates absent or incorrect style or severe instability. Preserve assesses source fidelity and temporal stability in the non-edit region: 5 indicates close, stable match, 3 allows minor changes or occasional jitter, and 0 indicates substantial repainting or severe drift. The two video-level scores are aggregated separately across cases. Prompt templates. The following template (Listing 2) retains the scoring rubric while making the edit direction explicit. For foreground editing, {target_region} is the foreground object inside the red outline; for background editing, it is the background outside the red outline. sections.content: This appendix specifies the training configuration of the reported GRNStyle-2B model, defines the checkpoint validation protocol, and discusses the observed validation trends. D.1 Training Setup Table 5 summarizes the main training configuration, which uses 100K paired examples across 18 style categories. The model is initialized from pre-trained GRNEdit [23] general-purpose video editor and fully fine-tunes the GRN-2B backbone and conditioning branches, while the video tokenizer and T5 encoder remain frozen. This initialization provides strong global stylization prior, so optimization primarily adapts the model to mask-guided local control rather than learning stylization from scratch. Training applies the all-token bit cross-entropy over the full video. With probability 0.50, the style-specific instruction is replaced by generic mask-following instruction, encouraging the model to read style identity from the polar style-aware mask while retaining text guidance. sections.title: F Global Stylization Comparison
sections.content: To test whether GRNStyle extends beyond local editing, we set the editing mask to all ones and apply the same checkpoint globally, without retraining. We compare with existing global video stylization methods (including StyleMaster [6], Ditto [21], EchoStyle [44], and PickStyle [27]) on the 80 benchmark videos and the same ten-style subset used in the main comparison. All methods follow the same frame-alignment and metric implementations. EchoStyle supports only five of the ten styles and is therefore evaluated on those five. Table 7 reports CSD, CLIPT, TC, and VLM-based Style score. GRNStyle obtains the highest CSD (0.683) and the second-highest VLM Style score (4.67). Its CLIPT (0.190) matches EchoStyle and is close to the best result (0.207), while its TC (0.977) remains competitive with the strongest methods. Notably, GRNStyle outperforms the 14B methods on CSD despite using 2B backbone, indicating that our style-aware conditioning transfers from local to global stylization without separate global model.

sections.title: G Robustness to Imperfect Masks
sections.content: We evaluate the robustness of GRNStyle to imperfect user-provided masks while keeping the source videos, style prompts, random seeds, guidance scale, and sampling configuration fixed. Starting from 40-case subset of the benchmark and ten styles, we obtain 400 videostyle evaluations for each variant. We consider five perturbation categories and evaluate each at light and strong severity levels: Boundary noise: pixels within six-pixel band around the mask contour are independently flipped with probability 0.15 (light) or 0.35 (strong) per frame. Dilation: the white edit region is expanded by fixed radius of 3 (light) or 9 (strong) pixels. Erosion: the white edit region is contracted by fixed radius of 3 (light) or 9 (strong) pixels. Temporal jitter: every frame receives an independently sampled signed radius in [3, 3] (light) or [9, 9] (strong) pixels. Frame dropout: the entire mask is cleared in approximately 10% (light) or 30% (strong) of frames. Radii are specified at 480p short side and scaled to the actual input resolution. The perturbed mask replaces the original mask in both the polar style encoding and the geometric support path; no retraining or parameter update is involved. Table 8 reports the results. Under light perturbations, all metrics remain close to the unperturbed baseline: absolute changes are within 0.006 for SPS and CLIPT and within 0.49 dB for PSNR, while TC remains at 0.972. Under strong perturbations, erosion and dropout produce the clearest reduction in stylization quality. Strong erosion lowers foreground SPS from 0.388 to 0.365, and strong dropout reduces background SPS from 0.677 to 0.599 and background CLIPT from 0.188 to 0.176. In contrast, strong dilation leaves the style-related metrics stable or slightly higher, but decreases background PSNR from 26.3 to 22.2 dB because the expanded edit region inevitably modifies content outside the original preserved area; its remaining metrics change little. Overall, GRNStyle remains robust to imperfect masks: style fidelity is largely preserved, and the remaining degradation is concentrated in the metric directly affected by each geometric perturbation.

sections.title: H Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Our current system has three notable limitations. First, temporal consistency can degrade for fast-moving objects, especially near motion boundaries. Rapid motion makes it difficult to maintain stable region alignment and coherent stylization across adjacent frames, which may lead to local flicker or inconsistent boundaries. Improving motion-aware conditioning and boundary tracking is an important direction for future work. Second, the data-construction pipeline relies on an object-removal model that may also remove the objects cast shadow. As result, some paired targets lack the original shadow even when it should remain semantically consistent with the scene. Training on such pairs can encourage the stylization model to erase shadows, producing visually unnatural results. Future work should improve shadow-aware data construction and incorporate explicit supervision for preserving scene-consistent shadows. Third, our evaluation suite does not include boundary-adherence metric, although boundary accuracy is an important aspect of local editing quality. Such metric is difficult to define in 29 practice: some styles intentionally expand the target object (e.g., Simpsons-style stylization) while others shrink it, so no single fixed boundary can serve as the ground truth for all outputs. Future work should develop style-aware boundary evaluation that distinguishes intended shape deformation from mask leakage and inadvertent boundary violations.
